newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge won't block key part of immigration law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge won't block key part of immigration law.

text.p: A federal judge on Friday refused to temporarily block a key part of the new immigration law that makes it easier for the United States to turn away some asylum seekers.

U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan rejected a request from a coalition of immigrant advocates seeking a temporary order blocking the expedited removal rules, which went into effect on April 1 as part of the tough new immigration law.

Sullivan promised a "prompt decision" on the merits of the underlying lawsuit challenging that one provision. He set a May 22 hearing for oral arguments and vowed to hand down a ruling soon after that session.

The groups challenged the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service rules allowing its agents to refuse entry at the border to individuals with improper documents unless a credible fear of persecution is found.
Under the new rules, immigration agents are not required to mention the right of asylum unless the person asks about it.

Asylum seekers previously were granted entry and given time to file a claim. Now immigration officials can decide the request immediately if the person has invalid or fraudulent documents, and court reviews of those decisions are limited.
The Justice Department, on behalf of the immigration agency, is defending the law.
Sullivan set a schedule for both sides to file court papers concerning requests for documents in April and to submit their basic arguments in May.

Paul Rubin, an attorney for the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights, one of the groups challenging the provision, said "thousands of people are going to be affected" by it. Sullivan agreed that the case presented significant issues.

The judge late on Monday granted a request from the groups to briefly delay implementation of the regulations, but a U.S. appeals court immediately overturned his decision, allowing the law to go into effect on schedule on April 1.

The law, approved by Congress and signed by President Bill Clinton in September, has created widespread confusion among immigrants in recent weeks and has prompted a number of court challenges around the country.
